description: Developer from Ankara with experience in computer vision, AI/ML, and data analysis. Building a data-driven, scientifically grounded project using NASA open data.
summary:
SPHEREx images the sky in 102 wavelengths, so every exposure of a star field is taken at a different wavelength. Played in time order, the raw exposures flicker so strongly that nothing can be seen moving. We built a public web tool that stacks the exposures of each observing epoch on a fixed sky grid and blinks the epoch stacks next to the raw frames. On constant field stars the flicker drops from 75–96% in the raw exposures to 1–2% in the epoch stacks, and nearby stars visibly move.

The tool also measures what it shows. For the brown dwarf Epsilon Indi B we measure a proper motion of 4.63 arcsec per year from SPHEREx images; the SIMBAD catalogue gives 4.68. The same fit, tested on 91 Gaia field stars and 10 fast-moving stars, is checked against the catalogues and the results are published on the site, including the cases where it fails. It is a first step towards searching SPHEREx data for nearby, unknown moving objects such as a distant Planet X.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Motion Viewer shows SPHEREx Level-2 images of a patch of sky in time order so that moving objects can be seen and measured.

- Images tab: one stacked image per observing epoch, blinked next to the raw exposures, with the catalogue position and a motion arrow. A long-wavelength view (detectors 5–6) shows cold objects such as the Y dwarf WISE 0855-0714.

- Measurement tab: proper motion and parallax fitted from the SPHEREx images with two position methods (ePSF fit and windowed centroid), aligned to Gaia field stars, compared with SIMBAD.

- Validation tab: the same fit run on 91 Gaia DR3 field stars and 10 fast-moving stars.

- Find the mover: a one-minute guided mode with three real targets, and a game mode with a score.

- Quick look: any star name or position, stacked live in the browser from the archive's cloud copy.

- 15 prepared targets, English and Turkish, keyboard controls.

HOW IT WORKS

SPHEREx takes each exposure at a different wavelength, so a star's brightness jumps from frame to frame. We put every exposure on a fixed sky grid (TAN-SIP projection), group them by observing epoch and stack each epoch. On constant field stars the median flicker falls from 75–96% (raw) to 1–2% (epoch stacks) across the five fields. Positions are measured per exposure and fitted with proper motion and parallax.

RESULTS

- Epsilon Indi B: 4.63 arcsec/yr measured, 4.68 arcsec/yr in SIMBAD.

- WISE 0855-0714: epoch 1→3 shift −7.97 / +1.08 arcsec measured against −8.01 / +0.65 predicted.

- 91 Gaia field stars: 75 within 2 errors in all three quantities, 79.1 expected for correct error bars.

- Fast movers: 8 of the 9 that could be judged agree with SIMBAD in both motion components.

Failures and limits are listed openly in the README: saturated targets (Barnard's Star in 357 of 364 exposures), a parallax 11% high for Epsilon Indi B, and an outage of the IRSA query service on 15 November 2026 during which the name search works only for a saved target.

WHY IT MATTERS

A nearby unknown object, from a brown dwarf to a hypothetical Planet X, would show up as motion between epochs. SPHEREx covers the whole sky every six months, so the same epoch-stacking method can be run on any field. Our tool shows that SPHEREx images are enough to measure stellar motion, checks that measurement against catalogues, and lets anyone see the motion with their own eyes.

TOOLS

Python 3.13 (astropy, numpy, scipy, pyvo, requests, pillow) for the data pipeline; React 19, TypeScript and Vite for the website; Vercel for hosting; Playwright for automated checks of the live site. Data: SPHEREx Level-2 images (NASA/IPAC IRSA), SIMBAD, Gaia DR3.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Inspired by WiseView, the blink tool for WISE data, but built for a problem specific to SPHEREx: every exposure is taken at a different wavelength. Every number on the site comes from a log or a data file, and failures are kept in the tables instead of hidden. The site is bilingual (English and Turkish) and needs no login, no install and no SI service.

Code and full documentation: https://github.com/FearmessOp/blackhole-spherex
